nirvana

nir-VAH-nuh -- three syllables, stress on the second syllable, VAH. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Nirvana is a state of happiness and peace.

With the twins finally asleep, the quiet porch felt like nirvana to their exhausted parents.

Example

All winter, the gardener shovels snow and scrapes ice. But inside the greenhouse it is nirvana -- seventy degrees and silent, tomatoes ripening in January, the only sound a slow drip of water -- and every worry stays outside the glass door.

Nirvana is a state of happiness and peace so complete that troubles cannot seem to reach it. In everyday English, nirvana names the perfect peace itself, wherever you find it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

serenity: Serenity is deep, untroubled calm -- a still lake at dawn, nothing stirring. Nirvana asks for more than calm: it is happiness and peace together, so complete that nothing hurts and nothing is missing. Serenity can exist without a single drop of joy.

bliss: Bliss is a rush of pure happiness -- the wave that floods you at a perfect moment, and often passes with it. Nirvana is quieter and more settled: not a wave of joy but a lasting state of peace that trouble cannot reach.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

torment: great suffering or distress

agony: extreme pain of body or mind

Where it sits · how complete the inner contentment is

contentment → nirvana → paradise

contentment vs. nirvana: Contentment is the everyday, weaker cousin of nirvana: you are satisfied with what you have, but ordinary worries still wait nearby. Nirvana leaves nothing to worry about at all.

paradise vs. nirvana: Paradise claims one step more than nirvana: nirvana perfects the state inside you, while paradise promises that everything -- the place, the weather, the whole world around you -- is perfect too.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — nir-: out, away (Sanskrit)

root — va-: to blow (Sanskrit vati)

suffix — -na: Sanskrit ending: 'having been' (Sanskrit)

Put it together: Nirvana is Sanskrit for 'a blowing out,' like a candle flame: nir- ('out') plus va ('to blow') plus the -na ending meaning 'having been' -- in Buddhism it names the blowing out of all suffering and craving. Everyday English borrowed the afterglow: a state of deep happiness and peace.

Use the root in a new word: nirvanic: Fans described the choir's final chord as almost nirvanic.

Word Building

Word Choice

In Buddhism, capital-N Nirvana is the ultimate release from suffering; in everyday English, lowercase nirvana is any state of perfect happiness and peace -- a hammock, a quiet cove, a greenhouse in January. Note the pace: euphoria races, but nirvana rests. If the joy is loud and electric, it is not nirvana.
